subject: physics

items.q: In which of these situations is work done on the object by the force described?
items.correct: A sledge is dragged forwards and slides 5 m over snow
items.misconception: A cleaner pushes hard on a crate that does not move
items.why: In everyday English 'work' means effort, and holding or straining is tiring, so students judge work by how hard the task feels rather than by whether the object moves. Work is done only when a force causes a displacement. With no movement s = 0, so W = F × 0 = 0 J however tiring the task is.
items.random_wrong: A waiter carries a tray level across a room

items.q: A student holds a box of weight 40 N still at chest height for 15 s. How much work does the student's upward force do on the box?
items.why: The symbol s is used for seconds as a unit and for distance as a quantity, and students pick whichever second number the question supplies. In W = F s the symbol s stands for distance in metres, not for time. Time never appears in the work done equation.

items.q: In the equation work done = force × distance, what is meant by the distance?
items.correct: The distance moved along the line of action of the force
items.misconception: The total length of the path that the object takes
items.why: Students read 'distance' as any distance travelled and ignore the bracket in the specification equation, which specifies distance moved along the line of action of the force. Only the distance moved along the line of action of the force counts. Horizontal movement is at right angles to a vertical force, so s = 0 for that force.
items.random_wrong: The distance the object moves, in any direction

items.q: A force of 25 N pushes a trolley 8 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done on the trolley?
items.why: Many GCSE equations students meet, such as speed = distance ÷ time and density = mass ÷ volume, are divisions, so division becomes the default operation when two numbers are given. W = F s is a multiplication: work done = force × distance. Dividing gives 3.125 or 0.32, neither of which is the work done.

items.q: A crane does 3000 J of work on a load using a force of 250 N. How far does the load move along the line of action of the force?
items.why: Students rearrange by moving symbols around by eye rather than by dividing both sides, so the two quantities on the right are easily swapped. Dividing both sides of W = F s by F gives s = W ÷ F. Check by substituting back: 250 × 12 = 3000 J.

items.q: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = F s?
items.correct: work in joules, force in newtons, distance in metres
items.misconception: work in newtons, force in newtons, distance in metres
items.why: The force is usually the number quoted in the question, and students carry its unit through to the answer without applying the equation, blurring the quantity force with the quantity work. In W = F s, force, F, is in newtons, N, and work done, W, is in joules, J. A force value on its own is never an amount of work.
items.random_wrong: work in watts, force in newtons, distance in metres

items.q: A motor does 6000 N m of work. What is this work done in joules?
items.why: Nearly every other conversion students meet (mm to m, g to kg, kJ to J) uses a factor of 10, 100 or 1000, so they expect a numerical factor here too. The newton-metre and the joule are two names for the same unit: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. Only the words change, so 6000 N m = 6000 J.

items.q: Which statement correctly defines one joule of work?
items.correct: The work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m
items.misconception: The work done when a force of 1 N acts for a time of 1 s
items.why: Students confuse the symbol s for distance with the abbreviation s for seconds, and they associate 'per second' definitions with the joule because of its link to the watt. The joule is defined through distance, not time: 1 N acting through a displacement of 1 m does 1 J of work. Energy per second is power, in watts.
items.random_wrong: The force of 1 N needed to move an object through 1 m

items.q: A crane lifts a steel beam steadily upwards. Which statement best describes what happens as the crane's force does work on the beam?
items.correct: Energy is transferred to the beam by the crane's force
items.misconception: New energy is created by the crane and passed to the beam
items.why: Students hear that doing work 'gives' an object energy and read that as making energy, especially where a fuel or a motor is involved. Doing work transfers energy from one store to another. The joules gained by the beam were already in another store; none are made.
items.random_wrong: Energy is used up by the crane, so none reaches it

items.q: A crate is pushed at a steady speed across a rough floor. What is the main effect of the work done against the frictional forces on the crate?
items.correct: The temperature of the crate rises steadily
items.misconception: The energy transferred is destroyed by friction
items.why: Everyday language talks about 'using up' energy and about friction 'wasting' it, and students cannot see where the energy has gone because nothing appears to happen. Energy is transferred, never destroyed. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic energy of the crate keeps rising

items.q: A student rubs their hands together quickly and the hands become warmer. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: Work is done against friction at the hands
items.misconception: The movement energy is used up and lost as heat
items.why: Everyday language talks about 'using up' energy and about friction 'wasting' it, and students cannot see where the energy has gone because nothing appears to happen. Energy is transferred, never destroyed. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.
items.random_wrong: Warm air trapped between the hands heats them

items.q: A force does 250 J of work on a trailer as the trailer is pulled along a track. What does this tell you?
items.correct: 250 J of energy has been transferred to it
items.misconception: 250 J of new energy was created by the pulling
items.why: Students hear that doing work 'gives' an object energy and read that as making energy, especially where a fuel or a motor is involved. Doing work transfers energy from one store to another. The joules gained by the beam were already in another store; none are made.
items.random_wrong: 250 J of energy was used up and cannot return

items.q: Why do bicycle brake blocks become hot when the bicycle is braked?
items.correct: Work is done against the frictional forces at the blocks, which causes a rise in their temperature.
items.misconception: Friction only slows things down; the warmth comes from the surrounding air rather than from the rubbing.
items.why: Friction is first taught purely as a force that opposes motion, so its heating effect is treated as a separate, unrelated fact. The same frictional force that opposes the motion also has work done against it, and that work raises the temperature of the object.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A force of 25 N moves a trolley 8 m. A student answers 33 J. What has gone wrong?
items.correct: They added the force and the distance instead of multiplying them; W = 25 × 8 = 200 J.
items.misconception: You combine the force and the distance by adding or subtracting them.
items.why: Under time pressure students combine the two given numbers with the easiest operation, and adding unlike quantities is not obviously wrong to them. Force and distance have different units and cannot be added or subtracted. The equation is a product: work done = force × distance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In W = F s, what does the symbol W stand for and what unit does it take?
items.correct: W stands for work done and is measured in joules, J.
items.misconception: W means watts, so the answer to a work calculation is in watts.
items.why: W is used as the abbreviation for the watt as well as the symbol for work done, and both appear in the same energy topic. Here W is the quantity work done, in joules, J. The watt is the unit of power, which is energy transferred per second.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.2 Work done and energy transfer
